title: BRICS Summit 2026: Who's Coming to New Delhi and What's at Stake for India
excerpt: Xi Jinping's first India visit since 2019, a Putin bilateral on defence and rare earths, and a consensus test after May's fractured communiqué — what to watch as Modi hosts 11-nation summit this week.
body:
• India hosts the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on September 12–13, with leaders from all 11 member nations expected to attend.
  • Chinese President Xi Jinping's likely visit would be his first trip to India since 2019, with a Modi-Xi bilateral meeting widely anticipated on the sidelines.
  • Russia's Kremlin said President Putin will hold talks with Modi on trade, rare earth cooperation and defence, with 90% of BRICS transactions already conducted in national currencies.
  • The summit faces a consensus test after the May foreign ministers' meeting failed to produce a joint communiqué for the first time during an Indian chairship year, fracturing over Middle East divisions.

India is set to host the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on September 12–13, bringing together leaders from across the expanded 11-member bloc in what will be the group's most consequential gathering since its 2024 enlargement. The summit marks 20 years since Brazil, Russia, India and China first formalised the grouping, and it arrives at a moment when the bloc's ability to maintain consensus faces its most serious test.

Who's in the Room

Prime Minister Narendra Modi will chair the summit under India's fourth BRICS presidency, themed "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability." The confirmed and expected attendee list reads like a who's who of the non-Western world: Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres is also likely to participate.

BRICS now comprises 11 full members — Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE — with ten partner countries from Belarus to Vietnam engaged in working-level tracks. According to Brazil's central bank, the expanded grouping accounts for roughly 49% of the world's population, 39% of global GDP and 23% of international trade.

The Bilateral Meetings That Could Matter Most

If Xi Jinping attends, it would be his first visit to India since the 2019 informal summit in Mamallapuram. The Chinese delegation could number around 400 officials, roughly double the 2019 contingent, according to media reports. Intense diplomatic preparation has preceded the visit, including the 25th round of Special Representative talks between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on August 28. A Modi-Xi bilateral on the sidelines is widely anticipated, touching on Line of Actual Control border management and trade imbalances.

"Putin will participate in the summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, where he will promote security, the economy, finance and culture."

— Dmitry Peskov, Kremlin spokesperson

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed on Tuesday that Putin will hold two-way talks with Modi, with trade, rare earth cooperation and the Sukhoi Su-57 stealth fighter jet on the bilateral agenda. Peskov also said 90% of transactions between Russia and BRICS nations are now conducted in national currencies, and that the issue of Russian firms accumulating excess Indian rupees is being "gradually resolved."

Modi-Pezeshkian discussions are expected to focus on the Chabahar Port corridor and Strait of Hormuz security, both directly relevant to India's energy and connectivity interests. The two leaders last met at the SCO summit in Bishkek on August 31 — their first meeting since the US-Iran war broke out.

India's Balancing Act

For India, the central challenge is keeping BRICS "non-Western" without letting it drift "anti-Western." The expanded bloc includes both Iran, which has pushed to rally opposition to US military action, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which maintain close security ties with Washington. India has resisted Russian and Iranian pushes to frame the group as an explicit counterweight to the United States, a stance necessary to protect New Delhi's parallel relationships with Washington, the Quad and European partners.

The clearest evidence of how fragile consensus has become came at the BRICS Foreign Ministers' Meeting in New Delhi in May, when ministers failed to produce a fully negotiated joint communiqué for the first time during an Indian chairship year. India issued a dual-track "Chair's Statement" with 63 negotiated paragraphs alongside explicitly recorded divergences. The fracture centred on West Asia, with Iran pushing for language condemning US-Israeli operations while Saudi Arabia and the UAE resisted framing BRICS as an anti-Western bloc, according to a Beats in Brief analysis.

What India Built During Its Chairship

Beyond the summit itself, India has convened more than 350 ministerial and working-group engagements across 25-plus cities in 2026. Concrete deliverables include a BRICS Global Value Chains Action Plan to integrate MSMEs into supply chains, proposals to link national fast-payment systems — India's UPI, Russia's SPFS and China's CIPS — for cheaper cross-border transactions, a Startup Innovation Hub, a Digital Agriculture Network and a Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids launched in Gurugram.

India has consistently framed payment interoperability as a practical efficiency tool rather than an anti-dollar political statement. Russia's Peskov reinforced this messaging on Tuesday, saying Moscow "does not seek de-dollarisation" and is "open to every acceptable method of payment."

What to Watch

Analysts are tracking three possible outcomes: a full consensus Joint Declaration covering political and economic tracks; a declaration heavy on economic deliverables but generalised on politically sensitive issues like the Middle East; or another failure to reach consensus, forcing reliance on a Chair's statement alone. The last scenario would signal deepening internal strain within the bloc.

Running alongside the diplomatic summit is the inaugural iBRICS Summit at The Oberoi, bringing together over 500 institutional investors including 250 sovereign wealth fund principals representing more than $1 trillion in combined assets. A "Sovereign Capital Compact" focused on critical minerals, renewable energy, ports and digital infrastructure is scheduled for signing on September 12.

For the Indian diaspora, the summit carries practical implications. India's exports to BRICS members were estimated at $82 billion in goods in FY2025–26 and $31.3 billion in services in 2024, according to Enso Group Managing Director Vaibhav Maloo. Sectors to watch include pharmaceuticals, engineering, digital services and energy security. Whether the summit produces a consensus declaration — or exposes the limits of an 11-member bloc navigating active conflicts among its own members — will shape not just India's diplomatic standing but the trade environment for Indian businesses worldwide.
